icyfox|next|

Some takes (and from talking to nvidia people):

- Delaware precedent in Caremark has a very high bar for culpability of boards in matters like this. So I suspect the combination of DoJ saying they won't prosecute combined with this standard will successfully remove their individual liability.

- I'm surprised this decision was completely unanimous at the board level, considering how they quickly forced him out. Full 180 in under two weeks.

- The news media is really confusing selling chips to Megaspeed then hosting them in Malaysia (giving chinese companies access - afaik still legal under the old export regime) and Megaspeed smuggling these physical chips for hosting in Chinese data centers. Former was legal and second was not.

- I would not be surprised if a pardon was mentioned at some point. Will be watching how state AGs end up getting involved. CA has already subpoenaed Nvidia for this.

- There was a drum circle at Nvidia from employees who were petitioning to get him back

Disclosure: I co-host a podcast that talks about this. More discussion if anyone is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8nLiELIhwA

glenngillen|parent|prev|next|

The podcast "The rest is classified", a podcast dedicated to spy agencies & stories about them, did an analysis of this situation. It's the most reasonable take IMO, and I'll attempt to provide an overly simplified version of what I took from it:

- Jensen doesn't appear to have done anything illegal - It seems unlikely Alice was a honeytrap in the standard definition of the term - Megaspeed + NVIDIA likely had a legitimate/legal commercial relationship, and the personal relationship grew from that. - Alice was quite public about her connection to Jensen on social media at the time - Given the way MSS (Chinese secret service operate) it is only logical they would then insert themselves in and exert influence over Alice's relationship - There's unlikely to be some scandal around secret smuggling of containers of processors. Jensen's economic interests and China's interests were already aligned. He's been trying to soften policy and allow more open trade. - For all the talk of intercepts, there's almost certainly no smoking gun of a direct message between Alice and an MSS handler. It'd be such a basic failure of spycraft, and it would have meant US agencies would have made a firmer statement around her status. - There's a disconnect between the conviction of the agency around this situation and what has been stated in the Rubio report

TLDR: this feels like a leveraged play from people who want a more hawkish approach to trade restrictions around AI. A salacious scandal about an affair with a spy makes front page news. A "data center in Singapore is letting Chinese nationals use GPUs" does not.

015UUZn8aEvW|prev|next|

One of the takeaways from this, and from the 2023 OpenAI saga, is that a firm's nominal governance structure isn't necessarily its real governance structure.

Note that I'm not making any judgement about whether Huang or Altman should have been fired. The point is that in both cases, the board members were nominally empowered to make that decision, and did make it, rightly or wrongly. But when the rubber hit the road, it turned out that there were other forces that overruled them.

This means that we should have some skepticism about governance mechanisms that haven't been tested, such as the one that Anthropic has set up. The idea that board members will actually be able to carry out decisions that have massive negative ramifications for major stakeholders turns out to be questionable in practice.

qdotme|root|parent|next|

Because of nonlinearities in the exponents.

Each win compounds faster than compounding of a loss. A near inverse of the Kelly criterion.

In mature markets (financial services in 2008) the risk is a zero sum game and there is no super-exponential compounding. In fact the opposite holds true - if you have more AUM your ability to extract proportionally more money from the market diminishes.

In the startup world, where you create new markets, Jevons paradox grants you that super-exponential growth.

Nvidia, SpaceX and probably a few others.. are the rare ones that are huge, and yet non-saturated market creators.

Apple is saturated. So is Meta, Netflix, Alphabet, etc.

Microsoft is a wildcard a bit with OpenAI stake, but.. maybe?

Amazon is habitually saturated but actually most adapted to it.

mrandish|root|parent|next|

Maybe it's just me, but in recent years I've noticed increasing confusion in threads like this from posters conflating, or failing to specify, which framework they're using to judge an action. We routinely mix up six distinct categories:

1. Legal / Statutory (which itself splits into four very different buckets: 1a. Criminal, 1b. Civil, 1c. Regulatory/Administrative and 1d. Legal Posture / Safe Harbor - actions which aren't illegal per se but forfeit or weaken a future defense)

2. Contractual / Corporate Policy (ToS, NDAs, employment contract, HR policy)

3. Professional Standards (fiduciary duty, engineering rigor, appropriate diligence, best practice norms)

4. Ethical (role and context-specific rules of conduct, whether explicitly codified or implicitly expected)

5. Moral (personal, religious or philosophical principles of right and wrong)

6. Social / Community Norms (unwritten expectations of etiquette or conduct in a subculture, role or context)

Evaluating a violation in any category greatly benefits from defining the relevant Scope - which should include a clear boundary, limit or jurisdiction where the rule applies (and, by exclusion, doesn't apply), Severity (a degree, extent or materiality threshold) and Intent (accident, negligence, malice or just plain stupidity). Those tend to matter when justifying the degree of any proposed consequence or corrective.

So far, nearly half the posts in this thread seem to be asserting one or more violations without clearly defining the category, scope and limits, so many of the responses are debating mismatches of either category, scope or limits. In a community of my fellow engineers, who I respect for the rigor and precision they bring to understanding systems and edge cases, that's surprising. There are so many interesting combinations of [Actors] x [Actions] x [Categories] x [Scopes] x [Consequences] to stress-test here, but we can't productively discuss them until we stop treating six different axes as a single binary.

ElProlactin|root|parent|next|

Section 18 covers false statements in documents filed with the SEC. Not applicable here.

Only the SEC can sue under Reg FD. It bans selective disclosure of material information to analysts or certain shareholders before the public hears it. An earnings call is the standard way companies disclose something broadly, so a statement on an earnings call is exactly the opposite of what this applies to.

Section 10(b)/Rule 10b-5 are very, very unlikely to be successful. "Does not intend" described the board's intent at the moment the statement was made. Case law makes it clear that a statement of intent or opinion is actionable only if the board didn't actually believe it.

The statement reinstating Huang indicated that the decision to bring him back was made after meetings with him and senior members of the US government. That indicates new information and events after November 17.

Unless you could prove that those meetings took place before the November 17 statement and that the statement was a lie (i.e. the board was actually considering bringing him back at the same time it told the public it wasn't), under the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 plaintiffs this wouldn't meet the bar required to survive a motion to dismiss.

Gemini, Claude, et. al. are not a substitute for actually thoroughly checking facts, and if you input a garbage prompt, you get a garbage output.

ElProlactin|root|parent|next|

> Meanwhile, the Board, charged with maximizing shareholder value, witnessed nearly half of that value evaporate in the wake of their decision.

With all due respect, I get that not everyone is a corporate lawyer and not everyone is interested in educating themselves about this subject, but it's lamentable that this simplistic and incorrect notion that boards are required to maximize stock price over all periods of time has become so widespread.

Nvidia is a Delaware corporation. Delaware case law makes it clear that directors are required to act in promoting the long-term corporate value and that they have broad discretion over day-to-day corporate strategy. Under Delaware's Business Judgment Rule, it is presumed that in making a business decision, directors act on an informed basis, in good faith and in the honest belief that the action taken was in the best interests of the company.

Rules around maximizing shareholder value in the short-term come into play when a company decides to sell itself, receives an offer to sell itself, is facing a takeover, etc. They do not apply to day-to-day matters.

Handling misconduct is a core duty of a board of directors and there is ample case law on this subject. A relevant one is DSM HoldCo, Inc. v. Demoulas, in which a popular CEO was fired and the Delaware Court of Chancery agreed that he was "an excellent operator" who delivered impressive financial results. It still sided with the board of directors under the Business Judgment Rule and concluded that financial performance does not make you unaccountable for misconduct.

Bottom line: the idea that "maximizing shareholder value" means boards cannot fire a CEO for misconduct if the stock price goes down is based on an uninformed understanding of what boards of directors are actually obligated to do under the law.

It's really annoying how many people throw around the nationalization word in internet postings. It's posted by:

1. People who have no clue or understanding of history.

2. People who have no clue or understanding of US law.

3. People who have no clue about the requirements of nationalization.

Or often people who are doing all three at the same time.

On those notes:

1. Nationalization has been used EXTREMELY rarely in US history and only in very extreme circumstances, and usually done with an eye toward saving a company from bankruptcy rather than forcing it to do something the government wants.

2. Under US law it is extremely difficult to nationalize a corporation even if the US government wanted to unless the corporate owners are also interested in nationalization.

3. In order to nationalize a corporation you would need to buy out the corporation, which means paying fair market value (often with a markup on top) which for mega valuations like Anthropic would be a "handout" of money from the US government on a scale never before seen.

It always comes down to fiduciary duty and the board is REQUIRED to do what is the best interest FOR THE SHAREHOLDERS. That's why someone's personal life doesn't matter as much when it comes to these sorts of things if the board believes they're the best person for the shareholders.

> It always comes down to fiduciary duty and the board is REQUIRED to do what is the best interest FOR THE SHAREHOLDERS.

In a very abstract sense. They can't act maliciously, but they can (and often do) take actions that, for example, prioritize less certain long-term gains over more certain short-term gains (or vice versa). A prime example may be a decision to buy another business or spin off a division, enter or exit a market, and yes, hire or fire a CEO. In all of these cases, shareholders can take a short-term hit or end up worse off in the long haul.

This is not a decision that was unlawful or that they couldn't defend in court. It's just that on second thought, they decided they like money more than they like principles, and the administration concurred.

dofm|root|parent|next|

There doesn't need to be a specific regulation mentioning specific chips, because high-powered GPUs are classified as export-controlled devices (like some high end CPUs are), and they have to be scored against the rules as such.

The US government specifies what kind of computation power will cross the threshold, based on expert advice about what kind of power is needed to achieve certain tasks the US government wishes to prevent. They revise these levels.

Their specifications are based around things like total processing power and density.

Then suppliers have to work it out for themselves or they are breaking the law.

They would already have been categorised as dual civilian-military use, but in 2023 BIS (Howard Lutnick's department as of 2025) changed the rules to tighten things further re: AI uses of chips.

PDF link, but here's some detail: https://www.wsgr.com/print/v2/content/49010598/BIS-Expands-E...

Nvidia's own compliance page is apparently here but their site is broken right now: https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/about-nvidia/company-policies/e...

All this is to say, if some new company in the USA sprang up with a GPU that was faster than an H200 (which needed specific intervention), then it would automatically be illegal to sell it to China without further permission; no new law would be necessary to ban it.

(Indeed, AMD may be in hot water too.)

None of this is controversial and there's no grey area: if a qualifying Nvidia GPU ends up in China, Nvidia are potentially on the hook for failing to control their exports, depending on the outcome of investigations.
